original_value: This paper describes a low-cost, small size, and high-sensitivity microwave sensor using a Complementary Circular Spiral Resonator (CCSR), which operates at around 2.4 GHz, for identifying liquid samples and determining their dielectric constants. The proposed sensor was fabricated and tested to effectively identify different liquids commonly used in daily life and determine the concentrations of various ethanol–water mixtures at by measuring the resonant frequency of the CCSR. Using acrylic paint, a square channel was drawn at the most sensitive position of the microwave sensor to ensure accuracy of the experiment. To estimate the dielectric constants of the liquids under test, an approximate model was established using a High-Frequency Simulator Structure (HFSS). The results obtained agree very well with the existing data. Two parabolic equations were calculated and fitted to identify unknown liquids and determine the concentrations of ethanol–water mixtures. Thus, our microwave sensor provides a method with high sensitivity and low consumption of material for liquid monitoring and determination, which proves the feasibility and broad prospect of this low-cost system in industrial application.

result.paraphrase: This paper presents a low-cost, compact, high-sensitivity microwave sensor based on a Complementary Circular Spiral Resonator (CCSR) operating at about 2.4 GHz for identifying liquid samples and measuring their dielectric constants. The fabricated sensor was tested to reliably distinguish commonly used everyday liquids and to determine the concentrations of various ethanol–water mixtures by monitoring the CCSR resonant frequency. A square channel was marked with acrylic paint at the sensor’s most sensitive location to ensure experimental accuracy. An approximate model built in High-Frequency Simulator Structure (HFSS) was used to estimate the dielectric constants of the liquids under test. The results matched the existing data very well. Two fitted parabolic equations were derived to identify unknown liquids and evaluate ethanol–water mixture concentrations. Overall, the microwave sensor offers a highly sensitive, low-material-consumption approach for liquid monitoring and analysis, demonstrating the feasibility and broad industrial potential of this low-cost system.
